topics.problem: Application code has bugs, and data arrives from many places. Tom could sign up twice because nothing said emails must be unique. A rule in the database is checked on every insert and update, from every program, every time.

topics.name: INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE
topics.definition: INSERT adds new rows, UPDATE changes values in existing rows, and DELETE removes rows — and both UPDATE and DELETE act on every row their WHERE matches, or on every row of the table if there is no WHERE.
topics.problem: A database is only useful if it can be kept up to date: new customers, price changes, cancelled orders. These three statements do all of that — and one missing WHERE can change or wipe every row, so they deserve care.

topics.name: Transactions and ACID
topics.definition: A transaction groups several statements into one all-or-nothing unit — BEGIN, then the changes, then COMMIT to keep them or ROLLBACK to undo them — and ACID names the four guarantees it gives: Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, Durable.
topics.problem: Moving money means taking £100 from one account and adding it to another. If the system crashes between the two, £100 vanishes. Transactions make sure either both changes happen or neither does — and that two people working at once don't corrupt each other's changes.

topics.name: Normalisation: designing tables that don't contradict themselves
topics.definition: Normalisation is designing tables so each fact is stored in exactly one place — usually to third normal form (3NF): one value per cell, and every column depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.
topics.problem: If every order row stored the customer's email, changing Priya's email means updating five rows — miss one and the database says two different things. That is an update anomaly. Normalisation designs it out, and it is a favourite interview question.

topics.name: Views: saved queries you can use like tables
topics.definition: A view is a named, saved SELECT that you query like a table; it stores no data of its own, so it always shows the current data, while a materialised view stores the result and must be refreshed.
topics.problem: The same "customer totals" query gets copied into ten reports, and when the rule changes, nine get fixed. A view keeps one definition in the database that everyone uses. Views can also hide columns people shouldn't see.

topics.name: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL — and DELETE versus TRUNCATE versus DROP
topics.definition: SQL commands fall into four families — DDL changes structure (CREATE, ALTER, DROP), DML changes data (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE), DCL controls access (GRANT, REVOKE) and TCL controls transactions (COMMIT, ROLLBACK) — and DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP remove rows, all rows, or the whole table.
topics.problem: "What is the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP?" is one of the most asked SQL theory questions. Knowing the four families answers it neatly, because the three belong to different families.

sql.title: Performance: indexes and query plans
sql.goal: Know why a query is slow, read the plan the database chose, and write queries and indexes that let it find rows without reading the whole table.

topics.name: Indexes: how a B-tree makes lookups fast
topics.definition: An index is a separate, sorted copy of one or more columns — usually a B-tree — with pointers back to the rows, so the database can jump to matching rows instead of scanning the whole table.
topics.problem: Without an index, `WHERE order_date = '2024-02-12'` must read every row and check it: a full table scan. On 100 million rows that is slow, and it gets slower as the table grows. An index turns it into a few quick steps.

topics.name: Reading a query plan with EXPLAIN
topics.definition: EXPLAIN shows the plan the database chose for a query — which tables it scans, which indexes it searches, how it joins and sorts — without (or, with ANALYZE, while) running it.
topics.problem: "This query is slow — what do you do?" The first answer is always: look at the plan. Guessing wastes time; the plan tells you whether the database is scanning a huge table, missing an index, or sorting millions of rows.

topics.name: Index-friendly queries: sargable filters and composite indexes
topics.definition: A filter is sargable when the database can use an index for it — the indexed column stands alone on one side of the comparison — and a composite index on (a, b) helps queries that filter on a, or on a and b, but not on b alone.
topics.problem: An index can exist and still not be used. `WHERE strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) = '2024-02'` reads every row even with an index on order_date. Knowing the rules lets you write the same filter in a way that uses the index.

topics.name: How a database runs a join: nested loop, hash join, merge join
topics.definition: Databases use three main join methods — a nested loop (for each row of one table, look up matches in the other), a hash join (build a hash table of one side, probe it with the other), and a merge join (walk two sorted inputs together) — and the optimiser picks one per join.
topics.problem: In senior interviews you may be asked why a join is slow or what a plan line like "Hash Join" means. Knowing the three methods tells you which index or memory setting will help.

sql.title: SQL interview problems, from easy to hard
sql.goal: Solve the classic SQL interview questions from a blank page, explain your approach while you write, and name the edge cases before the interviewer does.

topics.name: How to answer any SQL interview question
topics.definition: A repeatable method: restate the question, look at the tables and their grain, ask about edge cases, plan the steps out loud, write the query as small CTEs, then check the result against a few rows you can work out by hand.
topics.problem: Under pressure, people jump straight into typing, write one giant query, and miss the NULLs or ties the interviewer planted. Interviewers grade the process as much as the answer: do you clarify, structure, and verify?

topics.name: Quick-fire SQL theory questions
topics.definition: Short "what is the difference between…" questions that open many SQL interviews; each is best answered with a one-line definition of both sides, the key difference, and when you would use each.
topics.problem: These questions take thirty seconds each but set the tone for the interview. A crisp answer shows you really understand the tool; a vague one makes the interviewer dig deeper. They are collected here so you can revise them in one place.

topics.name: The second highest salary (and the Nth)
topics.definition: Return the second highest salary from employees. If there is no second highest salary, return NULL.
topics.problem: Whether you think about ties and about "no answer". LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1 is wrong when two people share the top salary, and many answers return no row at all instead of NULL.

topics.name: Employees who earn more than their manager
topics.definition: Find every employee who earns more than their own manager. Show the employee's name and salary, and the manager's name and salary.
topics.problem: Whether you can treat one table as two — a self join — and read a self-referencing key the right way round.

topics.name: Customers who have never had an order delivered
topics.definition: List every customer who has never had an order delivered — including customers who have never ordered at all.
topics.problem: Anti-joins, and the classic trap of putting a condition on the right-hand table in WHERE after a LEFT JOIN, which silently removes the customers you are looking for.

topics.name: Find duplicate emails, then remove the duplicates
topics.definition: Find every email that belongs to more than one customer, with how many sign-ups it has. Then delete the duplicates, keeping the row with the lowest customer_id.
topics.problem: GROUP BY with HAVING, the ROW_NUMBER pattern for picking one row per group, and writing a safe DELETE.

topics.name: The highest-paid employee in each department
topics.definition: For each department, return the employee (or employees, if tied) with the highest salary. Show the department name, the employee's name and their salary.
topics.problem: The most common window-function question: top N per group, including how to handle ties and how to filter on a window function.

topics.name: Employees paid above their department's average
topics.definition: List employees whose salary is above the average salary of their own department, showing that average next to them.
topics.problem: Comparing a row with an aggregate of its own group — three valid ways (window function, join to a grouped subquery, correlated subquery) and knowing when each fits.

topics.name: Month-over-month revenue growth
topics.definition: For each month, show the revenue and the percentage change from the previous month, rounded to one decimal place.
topics.problem: Aggregating to the right grain first, then LAG, then safe percentage maths — integer division and division by zero included.

topics.name: Each customer's first order
topics.definition: For each customer who has ordered, show their first order — its id, date and amount — and how many days after signing up they placed it.
topics.problem: Picking exactly one row per group (the first event per user) with ROW_NUMBER, and joining back for extra columns. Used for activation, onboarding and funnel questions.

topics.name: Streaks: orders on consecutive days (gaps and islands)
topics.definition: Find every streak where a customer ordered on two or more consecutive days. Show the customer, the first and last day of the streak, and its length in days.
topics.problem: The "gaps and islands" technique, which turns consecutive runs into groups — a favourite hard question for login streaks, consecutive wins and uninterrupted sessions.

topics.name: Products bought together
topics.definition: Find every pair of different products that appear in the same order, and count how many orders contain each pair. List each pair once.
topics.problem: A self join on a link table, and the trick for listing each pair once — the basis of "customers who bought this also bought…".

topics.name: Which products make up 80% of revenue? (share of total)
topics.definition: Show each product's revenue, its percentage of total revenue, and the running (cumulative) percentage from the best seller down. Then list the products that bring in the first 80% of revenue.
topics.problem: Window aggregates over the whole result (share of total), a running total with an explicit ROWS frame, and turning a cumulative share into a filter — the classic Pareto analysis.

topics.name: Retention: who came back within 30 days?
topics.definition: Of the customers who placed an order, what percentage placed another order within 30 days of their first one?
topics.problem: Cohort-style thinking: anchor each user on their first event, look for a later event within a window, and compute a rate — the core of product and growth analytics interviews.

topics.name: The median salary
topics.definition: Find the median salary of all employees, and then the median salary in each department.
topics.problem: Whether you can build a statistic that SQL doesn't always provide, using row numbers and counts — and handle both odd and even group sizes.

topics.name: Customers who bought every product in a category
topics.definition: Find the customers who have bought every product in the Stationery category.
topics.problem: "Every" questions — relational division — which can't be answered with a plain join. They test counting distinct matches against a total, or thinking in double negatives.

system_design.title: How system design interviews work
system_design.goal: Learn the step-by-step way to answer any design question before you learn the parts. Without a method, even good knowledge comes out messy under pressure.

topics.name: Meet the building blocks: a map of a typical web system
topics.definition: Most large web systems are built from the same dozen parts — clients, DNS, a CDN, load balancers, app servers, caches, databases, queues, workers and object storage — connected in a familiar shape.
topics.problem: System design questions use many technical words at once. If you don't know what each part does, answers sound like a list of jargon. Learning the map first makes every later topic easier, because each one is a closer look at one box on this map.

topics.name: The high-level design interview: a step-by-step answer framework
topics.definition: A repeatable order of steps for answering any 'Design X' question in about 45 minutes.
topics.problem: Under pressure, most people either freeze or start drawing boxes before they understand the question. Both lose marks. A fixed method gives you something to do in every minute, and shows the interviewer how you think.

topics.name: Back-of-the-envelope estimation
topics.definition: Quick, rough maths to estimate traffic, storage and bandwidth, so your design decisions are based on scale.
topics.problem: Without numbers you can't tell whether one server is enough or you need a hundred. Estimation turns a vague 'big app' into numbers that decide the design.

topics.name: The low-level design interview: a step-by-step approach
topics.definition: A repeatable way to answer 'Design the classes for X' (a parking lot, an elevator, Splitwise) and write the key code.
topics.problem: LLD questions are open-ended: 'design a parking lot' could mean almost anything. Without a method you write random classes, or code that breaks the moment the interviewer adds a requirement.

system_design.title: Networking and APIs
system_design.goal: Understand how a request travels from a phone or browser to your servers and back, and how to design the API it calls.

topics.name: Client–server, DNS, and what happens when you type a URL
topics.definition: Clients (browsers, apps) send requests; servers process them and send responses. DNS turns a name like example.com into an IP address the client can connect to.
topics.problem: Computers find each other by IP address, but people remember names. Between typing a name and seeing a page there are several steps, and each can be slow or fail. Knowing them lets you explain latency, failover and where caching helps.

topics.name: HTTP and REST API design
topics.definition: HTTP is the request–response protocol of the web. REST is a style of API design built around resources (nouns) and standard methods (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE).
topics.problem: Clients and servers are often built by different teams, or even different companies. They need a clear, stable contract for asking and answering; otherwise every change breaks somebody.

topics.name: Real-time communication: polling, long polling, WebSockets, SSE
topics.definition: Ways for a server to get new data to a client quickly: the client keeps asking (polling), waits on an open request (long polling), keeps a two-way connection open (WebSockets), or receives a one-way stream (server-sent events, SSE).
topics.problem: Normal HTTP lets the client ask but not the server tell. Chat, notifications, live prices and multiplayer games need updates pushed to the user within a fraction of a second.

topics.name: CDN (content delivery network)
topics.definition: A network of servers around the world that caches static content (images, video, scripts) close to users.
topics.problem: Distance costs time: a user in Sydney fetching from London waits around a quarter of a second for each round trip, and every byte you send costs bandwidth. Big files and users all over the world make this much worse.

topics.name: Proxies, reverse proxies and API gateways
topics.definition: A reverse proxy sits in front of your servers and receives requests on their behalf. An API gateway is a reverse proxy with API features: authentication, rate limiting and routing to the right service.
topics.problem: With many services, every client would need to know every service's address, and every service would repeat the same login checks, rate limits and logging. That's duplicated, inconsistent work.

system_design.title: Core concepts: scale, reliability and speed
system_design.goal: The ten ideas every high-level design uses: scalability, availability, fault tolerance, load balancing, caching, consistency and CAP, rate limiting, asynchronous processing, and observability.

topics.name: Scalability: vertical vs horizontal
topics.definition: Scalability is a system's ability to handle more load by adding resources.
topics.problem: A system that works for 100 users can fall over at 100,000. You need a way to add capacity without rewriting everything.

topics.name: Availability: nines, SLAs and redundancy
topics.definition: Availability is the share of time a system works and responds correctly, usually written in 'nines', like 99.9%.
topics.problem: Machines, disks, networks and whole datacentres fail. If your system has only one copy of anything important, that one failure takes everything down.

topics.name: Fault tolerance: timeouts, retries, circuit breakers
topics.definition: Fault tolerance means the system keeps working, perhaps in a reduced way, when parts of it fail.
topics.problem: In a system of many services, something is always slow or broken. Without protection, one slow dependency makes its callers wait, they run out of threads, and the failure spreads until everything is down.

topics.name: Load balancing
topics.definition: A load balancer spreads incoming requests across several servers and stops sending traffic to unhealthy ones.
topics.problem: One server can only handle so much, and if it dies, everyone using it is affected. You need to spread requests across many servers and route around the broken ones.

topics.name: Caching
topics.definition: A cache keeps a copy of frequently used data in fast storage, usually memory, so it can be served without repeating slow work.
topics.problem: Reading from a database on disk, or recalculating a result, is slow and expensive compared with reading memory. When the same data is read again and again, repeating the work is waste.

topics.name: Consistency, CAP and PACELC
topics.definition: Consistency (in distributed systems) means every read sees the latest write. The CAP theorem says that during a network partition, a system must choose between consistency and availability.
topics.problem: To survive failures and be fast for users everywhere, you keep copies of data on several machines. But copies can't all change at exactly the same instant, and the network between them can break. You must decide what users see in that gap.

topics.name: Rate limiting and backpressure
topics.definition: Rate limiting caps how many requests a client can make in a time window. Backpressure is a system telling the senders upstream to slow down when it's overloaded.
topics.problem: Without limits, one buggy script, scraper or attacker can send so many requests that everyone else gets errors. And a system that accepts more work than it can do eventually collapses for everyone.

topics.name: Asynchronous processing and message queues (Kafka, SQS)
topics.definition: Asynchronous processing means doing slow work later, outside the user's request. A message queue holds the work, or events, between the service that produces them and the services that consume them.
topics.problem: Some work is slow (encoding video, sending emails) or comes in bursts (a sale doubles traffic). Doing it inside the user's request makes them wait, and a burst can overwhelm the services behind it.

topics.name: Observability: logs, metrics and traces
topics.definition: Observability is how well you can understand what a system is doing from the outside, using logs, metrics and traces.
topics.problem: When something goes wrong in a system of many services, you can't attach a debugger to production. Without data coming out of the system, you're guessing.

system_design.title: Data: databases, storage and scaling data
system_design.goal: Choose the right database, keep data correct with transactions, make queries fast with indexes, and scale data with replication and sharding.

topics.name: SQL vs NoSQL: choosing a database
topics.definition: SQL (relational) databases store data in tables with a fixed schema and support joins and transactions. NoSQL is a family of other models: key-value, document, wide-column and graph.
topics.problem: Different data and different access patterns need different storage. A wrong choice hurts later: slow queries, joins you can't do, or a database that can't keep up with the writes.

topics.name: ACID transactions and isolation levels
topics.definition: A transaction groups several operations so they succeed or fail together. ACID stands for Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, Durable.
topics.problem: Real operations change several things at once: take money from A, give it to B. If the system crashes halfway, or two users act at the same moment, money can be created or destroyed.

topics.name: Database indexing
topics.definition: An index is an extra data structure that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table.
topics.problem: Finding one row among 100 million by checking every row takes seconds. Users and other services can't wait that long, and the database burns CPU doing it.

topics.name: Replication
topics.definition: Replication keeps copies of the same data on several machines.
topics.problem: One copy of your data is a single point of failure, and one machine can only answer so many reads. You need copies — and then you have to keep them in agreement.

topics.name: Partitioning and sharding
topics.definition: Sharding splits a large dataset across several databases (shards), each holding part of the data.
topics.problem: Even the biggest single database has limits on storage and write speed. When your data or writes outgrow it, you have to split the data across machines.

topics.name: Consistent hashing
topics.definition: Consistent hashing assigns keys to servers so that adding or removing a server moves only a small share of the keys.
topics.problem: If you place keys with hash(key) % N, adding or removing one server changes N and almost every key moves. For a cache, that means almost every request suddenly misses at once.

topics.name: Object storage (S3) for files and media
topics.definition: Object storage keeps files ('objects') such as images, videos and backups as a key pointing to bytes plus metadata, in a cheap, very durable, almost unlimited store like Amazon S3.
topics.problem: Photos, videos, backups and documents are big and numerous. Storing them in a database bloats it, slows backups and costs a lot; storing them on one server's disk breaks scaling.

topics.name: Search: inverted indexes and Elasticsearch
topics.definition: Full-text search finds the documents that contain some words and ranks them by relevance. It's built on an inverted index: a map from each word to the documents containing it.
topics.problem: Users type words, not IDs, and they expect the best matches first, even with typos. Normal database indexes can't do that efficiently.

topics.name: Unique ID generation
topics.definition: Generating IDs that are unique across many servers, without one shared database counter.
topics.problem: Every order, message and user needs an ID that never repeats. With many servers creating records at the same moment, one shared counter becomes a bottleneck and a single point of failure.

system_design.title: Distributed systems and security
system_design.goal: How services split up and stay correct across a network, how machines agree, and how to keep users and data secure.

topics.name: Monolith vs microservices
topics.definition: A monolith is one deployable application. Microservices split the system into small services, each owning one business capability and its own data, talking over the network.
topics.problem: As a product and team grow, one big codebase becomes slow to build, risky to deploy and hard for many teams to work on at once. But splitting it creates network and data problems.

topics.name: Distributed transactions: sagas and the outbox pattern
topics.definition: A saga runs a business process across several services as a series of local transactions, with a compensating action to undo each step if a later step fails.
topics.problem: An order needs stock reserved, a card charged and a shipment booked, in three different services with three databases. No single transaction can cover all three, but you still can't leave an order half done.

topics.name: Consensus and leader election (Raft)
topics.definition: Consensus is getting several machines to agree on a value — such as who the leader is, or the order of operations — even when some of them fail.
topics.problem: Several machines need to agree, even when some crash or messages are delayed. If two of them both believe they're in charge, data gets corrupted.

topics.name: Security basics: authentication, authorisation, OAuth and JWT
topics.definition: Authentication checks who you are. Authorisation checks what you're allowed to do.
topics.problem: Every system must know who is calling and what they may do, and must keep data safe even if something leaks. Mistakes here are the most expensive kind.

system_design.title: Low-level design: OOP and SOLID
system_design.goal: The building blocks of good class design: the four pillars of OOP, composition over inheritance, the five SOLID principles, class diagrams, and the concurrency basics LLD questions expect.

topics.name: OOP: the four pillars
topics.definition: Object-oriented programming organises code into objects that bundle data and behaviour. Its four pillars are encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism.
topics.problem: Large programs written as one long list of functions and shared variables become impossible to change safely. OOP groups data with the code that's allowed to change it.

topics.name: Composition over inheritance, and interfaces
topics.definition: Composition means building a class out of other objects it has ('has-a'), instead of inheriting from a parent ('is-a').
topics.problem: Inheritance looks like free reuse, but every subclass is tied to its parent's details. With several independent features, the number of subclasses explodes.

topics.name: SOLID: S — Single Responsibility Principle
topics.definition: A class should have one reason to change: one job.
topics.problem: When one class does several jobs, unrelated changes collide: a change to the email wording risks breaking the tax calculation, and every change means retesting everything.

topics.name: SOLID: O — Open/Closed Principle
topics.definition: Code should be open for extension but closed for modification: add new behaviour by adding code, not by editing code that already works.
topics.problem: Every time a new type of thing appears (a new payment method, a new discount), developers edit the same big if/else, and each edit risks breaking cases that already worked.

topics.name: SOLID: L — Liskov Substitution Principle
topics.definition: Objects of a subclass must work anywhere the parent class is expected, without breaking the program.
topics.problem: Polymorphism only works if every subtype really behaves like its parent. One misbehaving subclass forces callers to add special cases, and bugs appear far away from their cause.

topics.name: SOLID: I — Interface Segregation Principle
topics.definition: Clients shouldn't be forced to depend on methods they don't use. Prefer several small, focused interfaces over one big one.
topics.problem: Big 'do-everything' interfaces force classes to implement methods that make no sense for them, and every change to the big interface touches classes that don't care.

topics.name: SOLID: D — Dependency Inversion Principle
topics.definition: High-level code should depend on abstractions, not on concrete low-level details.
topics.problem: When business logic creates its own database connection or email client, it's welded to them. You can't test it without a real database, and switching providers means rewriting business code.

topics.name: UML class diagrams and relationships
topics.definition: A class diagram shows the classes, their fields and methods, and how they relate to each other.
topics.problem: In an interview, you need to show the structure of your design quickly, before coding. A clear diagram lets the interviewer follow you and correct you early.

topics.name: Concurrency basics: threads, locks and race conditions
topics.definition: Concurrency is several tasks making progress at the same time. A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the exact timing between them.
topics.problem: Real systems serve many users at once. When two of them change the same data at the same moment, results can be silently wrong, like one seat sold twice.

system_design.title: Design patterns
system_design.goal: Ten patterns that come up again and again in LLD interviews and real code: three for creating objects, three for structuring them, and four for behaviour.

topics.name: Singleton
topics.definition: Makes sure a class has only one instance, and gives one global way to reach it.
topics.problem: Some things should exist exactly once per program, like one configuration or one connection pool. Creating several wastes resources or causes conflicting settings.

topics.name: Factory: Factory Method and Abstract Factory
topics.definition: A factory creates objects for you, so the calling code asks for 'a notifier' without knowing which concrete class gets built.
topics.problem: If the code that uses an object also decides which concrete class to create, every new type means editing that code in many places.

topics.name: Builder
topics.definition: Builds a complex object step by step, instead of using a constructor with a dozen parameters.
topics.problem: Objects with many optional settings lead to long, confusing constructors, where it's easy to pass arguments in the wrong order.

topics.name: Adapter
topics.definition: Lets two incompatible interfaces work together, by wrapping one so it looks like the other.
topics.problem: You often need a library or old system whose interface doesn't match the one your code expects, and you can't (or shouldn't) change either side.

topics.name: Decorator
topics.definition: Adds behaviour to an object by wrapping it in another object with the same interface, without changing the original class.
topics.problem: You want to add extras like logging, caching or retries to some objects, in different combinations, without writing a subclass for every combination.

topics.name: Facade
topics.definition: Gives one simple interface to a complicated set of classes.
topics.problem: Using a complex subsystem directly means every caller must know many classes and the right order to call them, and that knowledge gets copied everywhere.

topics.name: Strategy
topics.definition: Puts a family of interchangeable algorithms behind one interface, so you can choose one at runtime.
topics.problem: When an algorithm can vary (pricing, sorting, routing), putting every variant in one method with if/else makes it long, hard to test and risky to extend.

topics.name: Observer
topics.definition: Lets objects subscribe to another object's events, and get notified automatically when something happens.
topics.problem: When one event must trigger several reactions, the code that raises the event ends up calling every reacting component directly, so adding a new reaction means editing it.

topics.name: Chain of Responsibility
topics.definition: Passes a request along a chain of handlers; each one either deals with it or passes it on to the next.
topics.problem: A request may need to pass several checks, or be handled by one of several handlers depending on its details. Hard-coding that sequence in one function makes it long and rigid.

topics.name: State
topics.definition: Lets an object change its behaviour when its internal state changes, by putting each state's behaviour in its own class.
topics.problem: Objects with modes (an order that's paid or shipped, a machine that's idle or dispensing) often end up with if/else on a status field in every method, and invalid actions slip through.

system_design.title: Low-level design questions
system_design.goal: Practise the classic LLD questions end to end: requirements, classes, patterns, the key code and concurrency.

topics.name: Design a parking lot
topics.definition: Design the classes for a multi-floor car park that assigns spots, issues tickets and charges fees.
topics.problem: It's the classic first LLD question: the entities are clear, there are natural places for patterns (pricing, spot assignment), and there's a real concurrency problem.

topics.name: Design an elevator system
topics.definition: Design the classes and scheduling logic for a building's lifts.
topics.problem: It tests state machines, scheduling and concurrency, and there's no single right answer, so your reasoning is what gets marked.

topics.name: Design Splitwise (expense sharing)
topics.definition: Design an expense-sharing app where friends split bills and can see who owes whom.
topics.problem: It tests clean modelling of money, validation, and a small algorithm (debt simplification), and it catches people who use floats for money.

topics.name: Design a vending machine
topics.definition: Design a vending machine that sells items, accepts coins and gives change.
topics.problem: It's the clearest test of the State pattern: every action means something different depending on the machine's state.

topics.name: Design an LRU cache
topics.definition: Design a fixed-size cache that removes the least recently used item when full, with get and put in O(1).
topics.problem: It tests data-structure design under a strict time limit (O(1) operations), and it's asked both as a coding question and as a design question.

topics.name: Design an order-matching engine (stock exchange)
topics.definition: Design the core of a stock exchange: an order book that matches buy and sell orders.
topics.problem: It tests data structures (heaps and queues), fairness rules, and why a single-threaded design can be both the fastest and the safest.

system_design.title: High-level design questions
system_design.goal: Practise the classic HLD questions with the full framework: requirements, estimates, API, data model, design, deep dives and trade-offs.

topics.name: Design a URL shortener (like bit.ly)
topics.definition: Turn long URLs into short links, like bit.ly/x7Kp2a, that redirect to the original.
topics.problem: It's the classic first HLD question: small enough to finish, and it covers APIs, unique IDs, caching, database choice and read-heavy scaling.

topics.name: Design a distributed rate limiter
topics.definition: A service that limits how many requests each client can make, enforced consistently across many API servers.
topics.problem: It tests algorithms (token bucket and windows), shared state across servers, atomic updates and failure handling, all in one small system.

topics.name: Design a notification system
topics.definition: Send notifications (mobile push, SMS, email) to users reliably, at large scale.
topics.problem: It tests queues, priorities, third-party integrations, retries and avoiding duplicates — everyday problems in real products.

topics.name: Design a chat app (like WhatsApp)
topics.definition: One-to-one and group messaging, with delivery receipts and online status.
topics.problem: It tests real-time connections, routing between servers, storage for enormous write volumes, ordering and offline delivery.

topics.name: Design a news feed (like Twitter or Instagram)
topics.definition: Show each user a feed of recent posts from the people they follow.
topics.problem: It tests the fan-out trade-off — do the work when posting or when reading — plus caching and the celebrity problem.

topics.name: Design a video streaming platform (like YouTube or Netflix)
topics.definition: Upload, process and stream videos to millions of viewers.
topics.problem: It tests large-file handling, background processing pipelines, CDNs and adaptive streaming — dealing with petabytes, not just requests.

topics.name: Design a ride-hailing app (like Uber)
topics.definition: Match riders with nearby drivers in real time, track trips and charge fares.
topics.problem: It tests geospatial search, very high-volume updates, real-time matching and preventing double-booking.

topics.name: Design a payment system
topics.definition: Process payments reliably: charge customers, record every money movement, and never lose money or charge twice.
topics.problem: It tests correctness under failure — retries, timeouts, idempotency, transactions and audit trails — where a small bug means real money.

topics.name: Design search autocomplete
topics.definition: Suggest the top completions as the user types into a search box.
topics.problem: It tests data structures at scale (tries), precomputing results, caching, and separating serving from data processing.

topics.name: Design a real-time leaderboard
topics.definition: Show live rankings of players by score, including each player's own rank.
topics.problem: It tests choosing the right data structure (a sorted set), and keeping a fast in-memory view in step with durable storage.

topics.name: Design a distributed cache
topics.definition: A shared in-memory key-value cache, like Redis or Memcached, spread across many machines.
topics.problem: It tests partitioning, consistent hashing, eviction, replication and failure handling — the building blocks of most large systems.

system_design.title: AI and ML system design
system_design.goal: The design questions AI and ML engineer interviews ask: RAG assistants, recommendations, fraud detection, LLM serving, and the pipeline that trains and ships models.

topics.name: Design a RAG assistant over company documents
topics.definition: A chat assistant that answers employees' questions from the company's own documents, with sources.
topics.problem: It's the most common AI-engineering design question: it tests retrieval, prompting, permissions, evaluation and cost control together.

topics.name: Design a recommendation system
topics.definition: Recommend items (videos, products, posts) that each user is likely to engage with.
topics.problem: It tests the two-stage pattern (retrieve, then rank), feature consistency, feedback loops, and how to measure success.

topics.name: Design a real-time fraud detection system
topics.definition: Score every card transaction for fraud within milliseconds, and block or flag the risky ones.
topics.problem: It tests real-time ML: low-latency features, imbalanced data, thresholds based on costs, labels that arrive late, and drift.

topics.name: Design an LLM serving platform
topics.definition: Serve large language models to many applications with low latency and cost.
topics.problem: It tests modern AI infrastructure: GPU cost, batching, memory limits, streaming, and fairness between teams.

topics.name: Design an ML training and feature pipeline
topics.definition: The platform that turns raw data into trained, deployed and monitored models, again and again.
topics.problem: It tests whether you see a model as a product with a lifecycle — data, features, training, deployment and monitoring — repeated forever.
